phenomenal consciousness is the part picked out by Nagel's question, whether there is something it is like for the subject to have the state. (Nagel, 1974) This is why the note lives next to [qualia](/thoughts/qualia) and [access consciousness](/thoughts/access-consciousness).

Block's distinction does the sorting work. Access consciousness is availability for reasoning, report, and action. Phenomenal consciousness is the experiential character of the state. (Block, 1995) A system can give strong access evidence while the phenomenal question stays open.

Chalmers calls discrimination, integration, report, attention, and control the easy problems because they are functional questions. (Chalmers, 1995) The hard problem asks why those functions come with experience at all. Levine names the same residue the explanatory gap. (Levine, 1983)

the test i want to keep:

- if an explanation only predicts report, memory, attention, or action, it is an access explanation.
- if it explains why seeing red feels this way from the inside, it is aimed at the phenomenal part.
- most [interpretability](/thoughts/mechanistic-interpretability) work is evidence of the first kind. It can show which internal state supports a report or decision. It needs another premise before it reaches phenomenal consciousness.
